By: Kate Barry | Paid

Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Asset Forfeiture Unit have been ordered to return R250 m worth of assets to the Guptas. What went wrong?

Press Release:


Gupta Assets
The National Prosecuting Authority was dealt a heavy blow in its State capture case against the Guptas, when the Free State High Court set aside the R250-million preservation order. The court found that there were shortcomings in the NPA’s case and no reasonable prospects of success in the prosecution.


Script:


GUPTA ASSETS

V/O: Last week another episode of the Estina Dairy Farm drama unfolded in the Bloemfontein High Court.

Judge: The provisional restraint order in respect of the first to the fifth applicants is discharged with costs, which costs include the costs of two counsel.

V/O: Judge Philip Loubser ordered the State to release a quarter of a billion Rands worth of Gupta-linked assets, allegedly ill-gotten in the Estina Dairy scam. In January we showed how money from the Free State Department of Agriculture, earmarked for emerging dairy farmers in Vrede, vanished into a feeding trough thousands of miles away from the platteland.

Pauli: The money would go from the Free State Department of Agriculture to this Estina. But from the Gupta Leaks and from the financials we could see the money went from Estina towards companies outside of South Africa and right back in towards the wedding in the end, and to Oakbay.

V/O: In February seven Gupta-linked associates appeared in Court facing criminal charges, including fraud, theft and contravening the Prevention of Organized Crime Act.

Link: The Gupta compound in Saxonwold has been like Grand Central station this year, with dawn raids, an arrest by the Hawks, and the seizure of luxury vehicles and other assets. But last week’s High Court ruling means that the to-ing and fro-ing will continue – because everything that was seized by the Asset Forfeiture Unit has to be given back.

V/O This multitude of assets included Porsches, Range Rovers, a Rolls Royce, a Bomb-ber-dier jet that is grounded at Lanseria, a Cessna aircraft, a Bell helicopter and dozens of properties across the country, including seven in the prestigious suburb of Saxonwold. But these can now be sold.

Richard: Every time the assets are unfrozen they get chipped away. The point is for this stuff not to be stolen in the first place. And we don’t have that capacity.

V/O; Richard Poplak is senior correspondent for the Daily Maverick, and has reported extensively on the GuptaLeaks.

Richard: Now in order to claw back some of what we’ve lost we can see that in the National Prosecuting Authority and elsewhere we don’t have the capacity to even do that. So we lose it on the front end and we lose it on the back end and the country is just bleeding and bleeding and bleeding due to corruption.

V/O: Richard believes that the capacity of state institutions like the NPA, the Hawks, the police, SARS, and even the Public Protector, have been deliberately eroded by Jacob Zuma.

Richard: Because over the course of the Zuma regime, what was the mandate? To gut all of the institutions that can act as a stopgap against corruption. So it shouldn’t be surprising to us. When you have a National Director of Public Prosecutions like Shaun Abrahams, who is still in his position, when he was clearly a Zuma loyalist, why should it be surprising to us that the capacity of the NPA has been gutted? And there’s one more element to this, that people tend to forget. The prosecutors are only as good as the investigations that are handed to them. So what does that say about the police? And in particular what does that say about the Hawks?
V/O: Indeed both Shaun Abrahams and the former Acting-Head of the Hawks, Lieutenant-General Matakata, were summoned to parliament to explain the delay in making arrests in the Estina matter.
Link 2: There have been two orders granted to the Asset Forfeiture Unit this year to freeze Gupta assets – one for R220 million, and another for R250 million. Both of these have been overturned by the Bloemfontein High Court, for roughly the same reason.
V/O: The NPA asserted that Estina director Kamal Vasram paid R110 million into an account at the Bank of Baroda, which then found its way to Oakbay. But the problem is that the Bank of Baroda account is a pool account servicing 750 clients.
Renee: Because it was the branch of a foreign bank in South Africa, that’s how it was registered, it wasn’t a fully-fledged Bank so it used Nedbank to have a current account, all the Bank of Baroda clients put their money in there, and then the money would flow out to which clients were then withdrawing.
V/O: Financial journalist Renee Bon-norchis has been reporting on the Bank of Baroda and the Guptas for Bloomberg.
Renee: The Judge said you know, you can’t see the direct flow - oh, it went from Estina to Bank of Baroda to Atul Gupta, he said you couldn’t see it. And when you look through the affidavit and actually the financial details of the accounts at the Bank of Baroda, you couldn’t see it. It, I presume, is enormously difficult to trace within a pool account.

V/O: But not impossible, with specialized forensic auditing.

Judge: It cannot be established that the amounts paid to Oakbay and Aerohaven flowed from the Estina deposits and not from the other deposits.

V/O: The Judge said there was insufficient evidence placed before him to uphold the order.

James: In essence, you can’t show me that I should believe you that the Guptas benefited here, and therefore I’m not going to confirm your order. That says nothing about whether there is the prospect of a criminal conviction.

Devi: But then that speaks to the State’s case?

James: On something which is irrelevant to criminal liability.

V/O: Advocate James Grant is a former professor of Law at Wits University.

Devi: How are going to find them guilty of a crime in all this?

James: So, for instance in the case of a theft: once you take that yogurt off a shelf in Pick n Pay and you walk outside with it, it doesn’t matter that you thereafter have a change of heart and return it to the shop, or that you manage to hide it in such a way that nobody can ever find it. The fact that you stole it, that you took it off a shelf and walked out without paying it is the theft and you can be prosecuted for that.

Link: So, what went wrong? Why did the NPA bungle the freezing of assets, and do they have the capacity to proceed with a successful prosecution? Unfortunately, they won’t give us any answers, because they weren’t available for an interview.

V/O: Instead they issued a media statement which perfectly demonstrates the problem. It states “the leadership of the NPA…have decided to wait for a formal judgment before deciding on available legal options.”
Surely you can’t get more formal than the Bloemfontein High Court?


Justin: “When are you going back to South Africa? The country’s looking for you.”
Justin: “Ajay! How you doing Sir?”

Ajay: “I’m fine, I’m fine.”

V/O: There’s a warrant for Ajay Gupta’s arrest and he’s been declared a fugitive from justice. But the Guptas, now living in Dubai, recently went on a religious pilgrimage to India They travelled through Rishikesh to Badrinath, where they donated gold plating for the roof of the Badrinath Temple, according to the Times of India.

Ajay: In my opinion there is no allegation at all in any part of the world. I’m sitting in India this moment, but I don’t know any allegation. But the media, the media has to give a reply then. Which allegation they talking?

Wayne: We know that there are serious concerns around the Guptas benefiting and profiteering from State money. It’s there. But it’s not just a case of baying for blood. It’s a case of asking the NPA and its Asset Forfeiture Unit to do the work properly.

V/O: OUTA’s Wayne Duvenage believes this setback is a good learning curve.

Wayne: The Estina matter is just one of many. We’ve got Transnet, we’ve got Prasa, we’ve got Eskom, there are so many matters that have to be attended to in terms of state capture, both in the Commission and the hearings, as well as the crimes that have to be undone and the undoing of state capture over time.

Richard: So organised crime in this country, like many countries, is completely entrenched. There are people who are going to do a lot more damage coming down the line. And there are people who are doing a lot of damage now. We need to have the capacity to fight that or we’re not going to survive. We can thank the Guptas for this, for warning us, for showing us the way. That’s what the Gupta Leaks did. They showed us what governments, corporations and corrupt entities, work in a sort of coherent triangle and siphon money off, very often legally, and very often illegally, from the state.
Link: The GuptaLeaks have shown us exactly how the State Capture project managed to loot billions of Rands of taxpayer’s money. This remains unchallenged. But knowing how it happened and who was involved is one thing: having the competence to prove it in a court of law is another.

Devi: Many South Africans have seen this as a loss, that if the Guptas are guilty of a crime they’re going to get away with it?

James: If as society we are after R250 million back from the Gupta’s and then we would be happy for them to walk away, well then yes, we might have lost. If on the other hand society wants justice and I think that’s what society really wants to see here, then we haven’t lost because the state is still perfectly on track with that. Well it’s nice to have R250 million back, yes. But, does it have anything to do with the prospect of a criminal conviction in respect of at least fraud, theft and corruption? Absolutely not - just in the same way that it doesn’t matter what colour socks the Guptas wear.
